vsm1.11:1.1:
Now comes the description of the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
which was listed as the “one perception” next to the immaterial states (III.105).
vsm1.11:1.2: Herein, it nourishes (āharati, lit. “brings on”), thus it is nutriment (āhāra, lit. “bringing on”).
vsm1.11:1.3:
That is of four kinds as: physical nutriment, nutriment consisting of contact, nutriment
consisting of mental volition, and nutriment consisting of consciousness.
vsm1.11:2.1: But what is it here that nourishes (brings on) what?
vsm1.11:2.2: Physical nutriment (kabaliṅkārāhāra) nourishes (brings on) the materiality of the octad that has nutritive essence as eighth:
vsm1.11:2.3: contact as nutriment nourishes (brings on) the three kinds of feeling;
vsm1.11:2.4: mental volition as nutriment nourishes (brings on) rebirth-linking in the three kinds of becoming;
vsm1.11:2.5: consciousness as nutriment nourishes (brings on) mentality-materiality at the moment of rebirth-linking.
vsm1.11:3.1:
Now, when there is physical nutriment there is attachment, which brings peril; when there is nutriment as contact there
is approaching, which brings peril; when there is nutriment as mental volition there is rebirth-linking, which brings
peril. And to show how they bring fear thus, physical nutriment should be illustrated by the simile of the child’s flesh (S II 98),
contact as nutriment by the simile of the hideless cow (S II 99), mental volition as nutriment by the simile of the pit of live
coals (S II 99), and consciousness as nutriment by the simile of the hundred spears (S II 100).
vsm1.11:4.1:
But of these four kinds of nutriment it is only physical nutriment, classed as what is eaten,
drunk, chewed, and tasted, that is intended here as “nutriment” in this sense.
vsm1.11:4.2: The perception arisen as the apprehension of the repulsive aspect in that nutriment is, “perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.”
vsm1.11:5.1:
One who wants to develop that perception of repulsiveness in nutriment should learn the meditation subject and see that he
has no uncertainty about even a single word of what he has learnt. Then he should go into solitary retreat and review repulsiveness
in ten aspects in the physical nutriment classified as what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, that is to say, as to going,
seeking, using, secretion, receptacle, what is uncooked (undigested), what is cooked (digested), fruit, outflow, and smearing.
vsm1.11:6.1:
1. Herein, as to going: even when a man has gone forth in so mighty a dispensation, still after he
has perhaps spent all night reciting the Enlightened One’s word or doing the ascetic’s work,
vsm1.11:6.2:
after he has risen early to do the duties connected with the shrine terrace and the Enlightenment-tree terrace, to set
out the water for drinking and washing, to sweep the grounds and to see to the needs of the body,
vsm1.11:6.3: after he has sat down on his seat and given attention to his meditation subject twenty or thirty times and got up again,
vsm1.11:6.4: then he must take his bowl and outer robe,
vsm1.11:6.5:
he must leave behind the ascetics’ woods that are not crowded with people, offer the bliss of seclusion,
possess shade and water, and are clean, cool, delightful places,
vsm1.11:6.6: he must disregard the Noble Ones’ delight in seclusion,
vsm1.11:6.7: and he must set out for the village in order to get nutriment, as a jackal for the charnel ground.
vsm1.11:7.1:
And as he goes thus, from the time when he steps down from his bed or chair he has to tread on a carpet
covered with the dust of his feet, geckos’ droppings, and so on.
vsm1.11:7.2:
Next he has to see the doorstep, which is more repulsive than the inside of the room since
it is often fouled with the droppings of rats, bats, and so on.
vsm1.11:7.3:
Next the lower terrace, which is more repulsive than the terrace above since it is all
smeared with the droppings of owls, pigeons, and so on.
vsm1.11:7.4:
Next the grounds, which are more repulsive than the lower floor since they are defiled by old grass and leaves blown
about by the wind, by sick novices’ urine, excrement, spittle and snot, and in the rainy season by water, mud, and so on.
vsm1.11:7.5: And he has to see the road to the monastery, which is more repulsive than the grounds.
vsm1.11:8.1:
In due course, after standing in the debating lodge when he has finished paying homage at the Enlightenment Tree and the shrine,
he sets out thinking, “Instead of looking at the shrine that is like a cluster of pearls, and the Enlightenment
Tree that is as lovely as a bouquet of peacock’s tail feathers, and the abode that is as fair as a god’s palace,
I must now turn my back on such a charming place and go abroad for the sake of food;”
vsm1.11:8.2:
and on the way to the village, the view of a road of stumps and thorns and an uneven
road broken up by the force of water awaits him.
vsm1.11:9.1:
Next, after he has put on his waist cloth as one who hides an abscess, and tied his waist band as one who ties
a bandage on a wound, and robed himself in his upper robes as one who hides a skeleton, and taken out his bowl as one who
takes out a pan for medicine, when he reaches the vicinity of the village gate, perhaps the sight of an elephant’s
carcass, a horse’s carcass, a buffalo’s carcass, a human carcass, a snake’s carcass, or a dog’s carcass awaits
him, and not only that, but he has to suffer his nose to be assailed by the smell of them.
vsm1.11:9.2:
Next, as he stands in the village gateway, he must scan the village streets in order to avoid
danger from savage elephants, horses, and so on.
vsm1.11:10.1:
So this repulsive experience beginning with the carpet that has to be trodden on and ending with the various kinds of carcasses
that have to be seen and smelled, has to be undergone for the sake of nutriment: “Oh, nutriment is indeed a repulsive thing!”
vsm1.11:10.2: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to going.
vsm1.11:11.2:
When he has endured the repulsiveness of going in this way, and has gone into the village, and is clothed in his cloak of patches,
he has to wander in the village streets from house to house like a beggar with a dish in his hand.
vsm1.11:11.3: And in the rainy season wherever he treads his feet sink into water and mire up to the flesh of the calves.
vsm1.11:11.4: He has to hold the bowl in one hand and his robe up with the other.
vsm1.11:11.5: In the hot season he has to go about with his body covered with the dirt, grass, and dust blown about by the wind.
vsm1.11:11.6:
On reaching such and such a house door he has to see and even to tread in gutters and cesspools covered with blue-bottles
and seething with all the species of worms, all mixed up with fish washings, meat washings, rice washings, spittle, snot, dogs’ and
pigs’ excrement, and what not, from which flies come up and settle on his outer cloak of patches and on his bowl and on his head.
vsm1.11:12.1: And when he enters a house, some give and some do not.
vsm1.11:12.2: And when they give, some give yesterday’s cooked rice and stale cakes and rancid jelly, sauce and so on.
vsm1.11:12.3: Some, not giving, say, “Please pass on, venerable sir,” others keep silent as if they did not see him.
vsm1.11:12.5: Others treat him with harsh words such as: “Go away, you bald-head.”
vsm1.11:12.6: When he has wandered for alms in the village in this way like a beggar, he has to depart from it.
vsm1.11:13.1:
So this experience beginning with the entry into the village and ending with the departure from it,
which is repulsive owing to the water, mud, etc., that has to be trodden in and seen and endured,
has to be undergone for the sake of nutriment: “Oh, nutriment is indeed a repulsive thing!”
vsm1.11:13.2: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to seeking.
vsm1.11:14.2:
After he has sought the nutriment in this way and is sitting at ease in a comfortable place outside the village,
then so long as he has not dipped his hand into it he would be able to invite a respected bhikkhu or a decent person, if he saw
one, to share it; but as soon as he has dipped his hand into it out of desire to eat he would be ashamed to say, “Take some.”
vsm1.11:14.3:
And when he has dipped his hand in and is squeezing it up, the sweat trickling down his five
fingers wets any dry crisp food there may be and makes it sodden.
vsm1.11:15.1:
And when its good appearance has been spoilt by his squeezing it up, and it has been made into a ball and put into his mouth,
then the lower teeth function as a mortar, the upper teeth as a pestle, and the tongue as a hand.
vsm1.11:15.2:
It gets pounded there with the pestle of the teeth like a dog’s dinner in a dog’s trough, while he turns it
over and over with his tongue; then the thin spittle at the tip of the tongue smears it, and the thick spittle behind
the middle of the tongue smears it, and the filth from the teeth in the parts where a tooth-stick cannot reach smears it.
vsm1.11:16.1:
When thus mashed up and besmeared, this peculiar compound now destitute of the original colour and smell
is reduced to a condition as utterly nauseating as a dog’s vomit in a dog’s trough.
vsm1.11:16.2: Yet, notwithstanding that it is like this, it can still be swallowed because it is no longer in range of the eye’s focus.
vsm1.11:16.3: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to using.
vsm1.11:17.2:
Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas and Wheel-turning Monarchs have only one of the four secretions
consisting of bile, phlegm, pus and blood, but those with weak merit have all four.
vsm1.11:17.3:
So when the food has arrived at the stage of being eaten and it enters inside, then in one whose secretion of bile
is in excess it becomes as utterly nauseating as if smeared with thick madhuka oil;
vsm1.11:17.4: in one whose secretion of phlegm in excess it is as if smeared with the juice of nāgabalā leaves;
vsm1.11:17.5: in one whose secretion of pus is in excess it is as if smeared with rancid buttermilk;
vsm1.11:17.6: and in one whose secretion of blood is in excess it is as utterly nauseating as if smeared with dye.
vsm1.11:17.7: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to secretion.
vsm1.11:18.2:
When it has gone inside the belly and is smeared with one of these secretions, then the receptacle
it goes into is no gold dish or crystal or silver dish and so on.
vsm1.11:18.3: On the contrary, if it is swallowed by one ten years old, it finds itself in a place like a cesspit unwashed for ten years.
vsm1.11:18.4:
If it is swallowed by one twenty years old, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety years old,
if it is swallowed by one a hundred years old, it finds itself in a place like a cesspit unwashed for a hundred years.
vsm1.11:18.5: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to receptacle.
vsm1.11:19.1: 6. How as to what is uncooked (undigested)?
vsm1.11:19.2:
After this nutriment has arrived at such a place for its receptacle, then for as long as it remains uncooked it stays in that same
place just described, which is shrouded in absolute darkness, pervaded by draughts, tainted by various smells of ordure and utterly
fetid and loathsome. And just as when a cloud out of season has rained during a drought and bits of grass and leaves
and rushes and the carcasses of snakes, dogs and human beings that have collected in a pit at the gate of an outcaste
village remain there warmed by the sun’s heat until the pit becomes covered with froth and bubbles, so too,
what has been swallowed that day and yesterday and the day before remains there together, and being smothered by the layer
of phlegm and covered with froth and bubbles produced by digestion through being fermented by the heat of the bodily fires,
it becomes quite loathsome. This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to what is uncooked.
vsm1.11:20.1: 7. How as to what is cooked?
vsm1.11:20.2:
When it has been completely cooked there by the bodily fires, it does not turn into gold,
silver, etc., as the ores of gold, silver, etc., do through smelting.
vsm1.11:20.3:
Instead, giving off froth and bubbles, it turns into excrement and fills the receptacle for digested food,
like brown clay squeezed with a smoothing trowel and packed into a tube, and it turns into urine and fills the bladder.
vsm1.11:20.4: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to what is cooked.
vsm1.11:21.2:
When it has been rightly cooked, it produces the various kinds of ordure consisting of head
hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, and the rest.
vsm1.11:21.3:
When wrongly cooked it produces the hundred diseases beginning with itch, ring-worm,
smallpox, leprosy, plague, consumption, coughs, flux, and so on.
vsm1.11:21.5: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to fruit.
vsm1.11:22.2:
On being swallowed, it enters by one door, after which it flows out by several doors in the way
beginning, “Eye-dirt from the eye, ear-dirt from the ear” (Sn 197).
vsm1.11:22.3: And on being swallowed it is swallowed even in the company of large gatherings.
vsm1.11:22.4: But on flowing out, now converted into excrement, urine, etc., it is excreted only in solitude.
vsm1.11:22.5: On the first day one is delighted to eat it, elated and full of happiness and joy.
vsm1.11:22.6: On the second day one stops one’s nose to void it, with a wry face, disgusted and dismayed.
vsm1.11:22.7: And on the first day one swallows it lustfully, greedily, gluttonously, infatuatedly.
vsm1.11:22.8: But on the second day, after a single night has passed, one excretes it with distaste, ashamed, humiliated and disgusted.
vsm1.11:23.1:
The food and drink so greatly prized—
The crisp to chew, the soft to suck—
Go in all by a single door,
But by nine doors come oozing out.

The food and drink so greatly prized—
The crisp to chew, the soft to suck—
Men like to eat in company,
But to excrete in secrecy.

The food and drink so greatly prized—
The crisp to chew, the soft to suck—
These a man eats with high delight,
And then excretes with dumb disgust.

The food and drink so greatly prized—
The crisp to chew, the soft to suck—
A single night will be enough
To bring them to putridity.
vsm1.11:23.2: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to outflow.
vsm1.11:24.2: At the time of using it he smears his hands, lips, tongue and palate, and they become repulsive by being smeared with it.
vsm1.11:24.3: And even when washed, they have to be washed again and again in order to remove the smell.
vsm1.11:24.4:
And, just as, when rice is being boiled, the husks, the red powder covering the grain, etc., rise up and smear the mouth,
rim and lid of the cauldron, so too, when eaten it rises up during its cooking and simmering by the bodily
fire that pervades the whole body, it turns into tartar, which smears the teeth, and it turns into spittle,
phlegm, etc., which respectively smear the tongue, palate, etc.; and it turns into eye-dirt, ear-dirt, snot,
urine, excrement, etc., which respectively smear the eyes, ears, nose and nether passages.
vsm1.11:24.5: And when these doors are smeared by it, they never become either clean or pleasing even though washed every day.
vsm1.11:24.6: And after one has washed a certain one of these, the hand has to be washed again.
vsm1.11:24.7:
And after one has washed a certain one of these, the repulsiveness does not depart from it even
after two or three washings with cow dung and clay and scented powder.
vsm1.11:24.8: This is how repulsiveness should be reviewed as to smearing.
vsm1.11:25.1:
As he reviews repulsiveness in this way in ten aspects and strikes at it with thought and applied thought,
physical nutriment becomes evident to him in its repulsive aspect.
vsm1.11:25.2: He cultivates that sign again and again, develops and repeatedly practices it.
vsm1.11:25.3:
As he does so, the hindrances are suppressed, and his mind is concentrated in access concentration, but without
reaching absorption because of the profundity of physical nutriment as a state with an individual essence.
vsm1.11:25.4:
But perception is evident here in the apprehension of the repulsive aspect, which is why this
meditation subject goes by the name of “perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.”
vsm1.11:26.1:
When a bhikkhu devotes himself to this perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
his mind retreats, retracts and recoils from craving for flavours.
vsm1.11:26.2:
He nourishes himself with nutriment without vanity and only for the purpose of crossing over suffering,
as one who seeks to cross over the desert eats his own dead child’s flesh (S II 98).
vsm1.11:26.3:
Then his greed for the five cords of sense desire comes to be fully understood without
difficulty by means of the full understanding of the physical nutriment.
vsm1.11:26.4: He fully understands the materiality aggregate by means of the full-understanding of the five cords of sense desire.
vsm1.11:26.5:
Development of mindfulness occupied with the body comes to perfection in him through
the repulsiveness of “what is uncooked” and the rest.
vsm1.11:26.6: He has entered upon a way that is in conformity with the perception of foulness.
vsm1.11:26.7:
And by keeping to this way, even if he does not experience the deathless goal in this life,
he is at least bound for a happy destiny.
vsm1.11:26.8: This is the detailed explanation of the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.
